newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada says new infrastrure plan won't hurt budget.
newsitem.headline: Canada says new infrastrure plan won't hurt budget.

text.p: Plans to expand Canada's exisiting infrastructure program in 1997 will not jeopardise the Liberal government's deficit reduction targets, Treasury Board President Marcel Masse said on Tuesday.

"The money is within our fiscal framework," Masse told reporters after a cabinet meeting. "The fact that interest rates have been lower and lower than expected in our forecasts, gives us room for manouvre that will permit us to finance the continuation of the infrastructure program while keeping our projections in terms of the deficit and not increasing the debt."
Earlier on Tuesday Ottawa said it had offered to put up a further C$425 million to extend the country's infrastructure program in 1997 and create up to 20,000 jobs.
The government's offer would add to the C$175 million budgeted under the existing program, begun soon after the Liberals came to power in 1993.

When combined with contributions of provinces and local governments, the federal offer could create infrastructure investments of about C$1.8 billion across Canada in 1997, a government statement said.

"Our proposal could support about 2,500 new projects across the country and create between 15,000 and 20,000 jobs in the construction sector and the construction-related industries," Masse, who is also the minister responsible for infrastructure, said in a statement issued earlier.

Finance Minister Paul Martin has pledged to reduce the country's deficit to C$24.3 billion in fiscal 1996/97 (April-March) and C$17.0 billion in 1997/98. The 1996/97 budget contains a C$2.5 billion contingency reserve. Ottawa plans to put aside C$3.0 billion for unexpected needs in fiscal 1997/98.
